summary: The developer machine has everything required to start building the Node.js + Mongoose multi-tenant sample and verify it against the live Azure DocumentDB cluster: Node 24, npx, Docker, az (signed-in), the service-specific documentdb MCP server, and the Microsoft Learn documentation MCP server are available, plus a rich set of installed documentdb-* agent skills. Missing CLIs (azd, bicep, terraform, dotnet) and mongosh are not blocking (workarounds exist through the documentdb MCP server and the provided skills). Several cold answers from the model were outdated or confused with Azure Cosmos DB (RU) or other neighbors — the report lists each mismatch, the correct facts with grounding links, the build risk if the wrong fact were used, and concrete doc/skill edits to prevent the confusion.
summary_points: Ready to start: Node 24, npx, Docker, az (signed-in), the documentdb data-plane MCP server, and Microsoft Learn MCP server are present along with many documentdb-* skills needed to implement and verify the sample.
Verdict is ready_with_gaps because some useful CLIs are missing from PATH (azd, bicep, terraform, dotnet) and mongosh is absent; none are blocking due to available workarounds.

Several cold answers were incorrect or outdated because the model mixed this service up with older Cosmos DB resource models or with other vendors — the biggest mismatches were the ARM resource type (use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters, not databaseAccounts) and the billing model (vCore/tiers, not RU/s).
The documentdb MCP server plus the documentdb-* skills and Microsoft Learn docs provide authoritative grounding for corrections and for repository / connection / index guidance.

Inventory recommendations advise adding optional developer tools (azd, bicep, terraform, dotnet, mongosh) only if the team wants local convenience; instructions and workarounds are given so an agent can proceed without them.

Action items for the product team: mark or deprecate older Cosmos DB pages that still use databaseAccounts for this product; add a short note to 'connect' quickstarts to distinguish Cosmos DB (RU) and the new DocumentDB vCore clusters.

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Resource type for an account/cluster: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (the logical "Cosmos DB account" resource).
confusions.grounded_answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Resource type for a managed DocumentDB cluster: Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (not Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts).

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters (ARM/Terraform templates)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The model answered with the historical Cosmos DB 'databaseAccounts' resource shape (used by the older Cosmos DB account APIs). The new vCore-managed Mongo clusters are a distinct resource type: Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters.

confusion_sources.title: Some Cosmos DB samples and older docs that describe Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts

confusions.build_risk: If the builder used databaseAccounts in templates/ARM/Bicep, they'd attempt to create or modify the wrong resource type and fail to manage the vCore cluster (or accidentally target a different service namespace).
improvements: On the main quickstart pages (e.g., Quickstart: Create a cluster), add a one-line note: 'This product uses Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters; do not use Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (Cosmos DB account) for vCore clusters.'
Deprecate or add a prominent 'different product' banner on older pages that still reference databaseAccounts for Mongo deployments.

confusions.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the built-in 'az cosmosdb' command group. Example to create: az cosmosdb create ... This is in the core az CLI (not a third-party extension).
confusions.grounded_answer: The primary command group for vCore DocumentDB clusters is 'az documentdb mongocluster' (provided by the documentdb CLI extension). There is also a 'az cosmosdb mongocluster' command surface in docs for compatibility in some versions, but 'az documentdb mongocluster' and the documentdb extension/command group is the current surface used in the official quickstarts.

grounding_links.title: az documentdb mongocluster (Azure CLI docs)
Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The model used the older/common 'az cosmosdb' command group that manages Cosmos DB account resources; the new vCore cluster surface is surfaced as 'documentdb' (an extension command group) in current docs.

confusion_sources.title: az cosmosdb mongocluster docs (compat or older surfaces)

confusions.build_risk: Using az cosmosdb create with --kind MongoDB targets a different management surface (Cosmos DB RU accounts) and could provision the wrong account type or produce incompatible connection strings; automation scripts would fail to manage the provided vCore clusters.
improvements: Clarify the CLI quickstart: add an explicit 'use az extension add --name documentdb' step and show 'az documentdb mongocluster' commands as the canonical surface.
Add a short comparison table on the CLI quickstart showing 'az documentdb' vs 'az cosmosdb' and when to use each.

confusions.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Bicep/ARM: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts. Terraform (azurerm provider): azurerm_cosmosdb_account (for the account) and azurerm_cosmosdb_mongo_database / azurerm_cosmosdb_mongo_collection for DB/collections.
confusions.grounded_answer: Use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters for Bicep/ARM (and the corresponding Terraform/AzAPI entries). The vCore 'mongo cluster' is a distinct resource type (Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters). The older azurerm_cosmosdb_account resources and Cosmos DB RU resources are not the correct target for a DocumentDB vCore mongoClusters deployment.

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters (ARM/Terraform templates)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer reused the older Cosmos DB ARM/Terraform resource names (databaseAccounts / azurerm_cosmosdb_account) which apply to Cosmos DB RU accounts, not the newer mongoClusters vCore resource.

confusion_sources.title: Terraform azurerm_cosmosdb_account docs (applies to Cosmos DB accounts)

confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong ARM/Terraform resource will cause failed deployments or create an account with different billing/throughput semantics; IaC in the repo would be invalid for the target cluster.
improvements: Add a Bicep/Terraform quickstart example for Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters near the CLI quickstart and highlight the distinction from databaseAccounts.
Add a one-line migration note in the Azure docs: 'If you need a vCore mongo cluster, use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters; do not use databaseAccounts.'

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer: Scheme: mongodb:// or mongodb+srv:// (MongoDB drivers). Host suffix for Cosmos Mongo API: <account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com (or SRV entry on that domain). TLS/SSL port commonly 10255 for non-SRV TLS connections. Typical example: mongodb://myUser:myPassword@myaccount.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/myDatabase?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false. Use tls/ssl=true, replicaSet=globaldb and retryWrites=false in the query string for Cosmos Mongo API connections.
confusions.grounded_answer: DocumentDB (vCore mongoClusters) uses SRV or standard Mongo connection strings with hostnames like <cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com (SRV style: mongodb+srv://...) and the service commonly recommends mongodb+srv with TLS and authMechanism=SCRAM-SHA-256; SRV obviates explicit port. The cluster's quickstart and GetConnectionStrings list examples such as mongodb+srv://<user>:<password>@myCluster.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com/?tls=true&authMechanism=SCRAM-SHA-256&retrywrites=false&maxIdleTimeMS=120000.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Use Azure DocumentDB with MongoDB driver for Node.js (connection string example)
Get-AzDocumentDBMongoClusterConnectionString example (PowerShell output)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The model produced a Cosmos DB (RU) style host suffix (.mongo.cosmos.azure.com) and the commonly-cited port 10255 used by Cosmos account endpoints. The vCore clusters use a different host shape (mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com) and vanilla SRV-based strings in the quickstarts.

confusion_sources.title: Cosmos DB Mongo API connection string docs (older Cosmos RU samples)

confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong host suffix or assumptions about port 10255 can make the sample fail to connect or attempt insecure options. Automated parsing/validation of DOCUMENTDB_URI could incorrectly modify a correct SRV string.
improvements: On the 'Get connection strings' quickstart page, add a one-line canonical example for vCore clusters with SRV hostname (e.g., 'mongodb+srv://<user>:<pass>@<cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com/?tls=true&authMechanism=SCRAM-SHA-256').
Add a short FAQ blurb distinguishing 'host suffixes and ports used by Cosmos DB RU vs DocumentDB vCore clusters' on the connection docs.

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: Capacity is billed as Azure Cosmos DB throughput (Request Units per second, RU/s) ... not a simple vCore tier for the classic Mongo API accounts (billing is RU-based).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (vCore mongoClusters) is a vCore / compute-tier based product (tiers like M30, M40 etc.) — you choose a compute tier (vCores) and storage; it is not billed as RU/s. RU-based (request-unit) billing applies to Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (RU) accounts (a different service).

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI (shows --tier M30)
What is Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)? (naming & billing summary)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The model recalled Cosmos DB RU billing (common for Cosmos Mongo API) and applied it to the vCore DocumentDB offering; the two services have different billing models.

confusion_sources.title: Azure Cosmos DB RU-based throughput docs (can be confused with Mongo RU accounts)

confusions.build_risk: If the sample's README or IaC assumed RU/s, builders might produce incorrect cost guidance and attempt to set RU throughput on a vCore cluster, causing provisioning errors or unexpected billing.
improvements: Add a clear 'Pricing model' note on the Cluster quickstart and overview: 'vCore compute tiers (M30 etc.) + storage — not RU/s; RU-based Cosmos DB is a different product.'
Show a short snippet in the quickstart that prints the cluster tier and billing model returned by 'az documentdb mongocluster show'.

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: Primary supported auth for the MongoDB API is MongoDB-style user/password (SCRAM) using the account keys or database users ... There is no widely used out-of-the-box flow where a MongoDB driver directly performs AAD/OAuth authentication against the Mongo endpoint.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports both native (SCRAM) authentication and Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) authentication for data-plane connections. When Microsoft Entra ID auth is enabled on the cluster, drivers can authenticate by presenting an Entra-issued OIDC access token (the docs provide examples and instructions for enabling 'MicrosoftEntraID' in the cluster's authConfig and for driver OIDC integration).

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The model assumed the older behavior where drivers used only SCRAM; the current vCore clusters support Microsoft Entra ID (OIDC) as a first-class authentication method when enabled.
confusions.build_risk: If the sample forced password-only flows, it would miss the recommended managed identity / AAD credential path for production clusters; conversely, attempting Entra-based auth without enabling the cluster would fail.
improvements: Add a small snippet in the Mongoose quickstart showing both password and Entra OIDC connection code paths and the 'az documentdb mongocluster update --auth-allowed-modes' command to toggle MicrosoftEntraID.
Document in the tutorial when Entra auth is a paid-tier capability and how to enable it in a single short section.

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the standard MongoDB drivers (e.g., the official MongoDB Node.js driver) and Mongoose for Node.js. There is not a separate "DocumentDB Mongo" driver; the service implements the MongoDB wire protocol so use the official Mongo/Mongoose client libraries.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct — use standard MongoDB drivers and Mongoose. Microsoft documentation and quickstarts show Mongoose and the mongodb driver being used with Azure DocumentDB clusters (examples and tested driver versions are provided).

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Connect Mongoose to Azure DocumentDB (official tutorial)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: n/a

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: I expect support for common vector index types such as HNSW, IVF and DiskANN on vector-capable clusters. A Mongo-like createIndex command would look like: db.products.createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { name: 'emb_idx', vectorIndexType: 'hnsw', similarity: 'cosine', dimensions: 1536, 'hnswOptions': { M:16, efConstruction:200 } }). (This is my best practical guess at the index options/syntax.)
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports IVFFLAT (vector-ivf), HNSW (vector-hnsw) and DiskANN (vector-diskann). Indexes are created via the collection-level createIndexes/createIndex mechanism but using cosmosSearch/cosmosSearchOptions payloads (e.g. specifying 'kind': 'vector-hnsw' or 'vector-ivf' and associated parameters like dimensions, m/efConstruction, numLists, similarity). The service exposes $search with the 'cosmosSearch' operator for queries.

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (IVF/HNSW/DiskANN examples & params)
Example using an HNSW index

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The model guessed a MongoDB-style driver createIndex payload shape and options; DocumentDB uses a 'cosmosSearchOptions' structure and specific 'kind' values rather than the guessed 'vectorIndexType' syntax.
confusions.build_risk: If the sample attempted to create vector indexes with the guessed option names, index creation would fail. This would break any vector-search examples or tests.
improvements: Add a short 'Create a vector index' example in the Node/Mongoose quickstart that shows the exact createIndexes payload with cosmosSearchOptions and the 'kind' field for HNSW/IVF/DiskANN.
Include a one-line mapping table: 'algorithms: kind values' (HNSW -> vector-hnsw, IVF -> vector-ivf, DiskANN -> vector-diskann) near the vector-search docs.

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: Full-text search is typically handled by integrating Azure Cognitive Search ... The MongoDB API itself does not provide Atlas Search; use an Azure search layer for advanced text or hybrid search.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB includes built-in full-text and hybrid search via the createSearchIndexes command and the $search aggregation stage (the 'cosmosSearch' operator). You can perform BM25 full-text queries and combine lexical search and vector search in a single $search pipeline (hybrid search) without provisioning a separate Azure Cognitive Search service.

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store & cosmosSearch / $search hybrid search (vector + lexical)
documentdb-full-text-search skill (createSearchIndexes and $search)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The model assumed Atlas-like or external search integration patterns (Azure Cognitive Search) instead of the service's integrated search + vector capabilities exposed through the $search/cosmosSearch operator.

confusion_sources.title: Generic guidance to use Azure Cognitive Search for Cosmos DB classic

confusions.build_risk: If the builder modeled the sample to ETL data into a separate search service, they would add unnecessary complexity and cost. They would also miss the integrated $search capabilities required for the sample's hybrid-search demonstrations.
improvements: Add a clear 'Built-in search' section to the quickstart that demonstrates creating a text index and a hybrid $search that uses both text and vector scoring.
Add a short note in the 'Use Mongoose' tutorial clarifying that integrated search exists and what features are supported vs. using Azure Cognitive Search.

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: Cosmos DB's MongoDB API supports specific MongoDB server versions/wire protocol levels (customers typically choose a server-version compatibility like 3.6/4.0/4.2/4.4/5.0/6.0/7.0 depending on account). Some advanced MongoDB features may be limited or not supported ...
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports MongoDB wire protocol versions 5.0, 6.0, 7.0 and 8.0 and documents that ~99% of MQL operators are supported. It excludes some admin commands and certain platform-managed operations; see the MQL compatibility reference for the operator-by-operator support matrix.

grounding_links.title: MongoDB Query Language (MQL) compatibility in Azure DocumentDB (operators & versions)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The model gave an older-style answer suggesting older compatibility choices and vagueness; the current product documents explicit supported protocol versions (5.0–8.0) and enumerates unsupported admin commands.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumed a different wire version than the cluster supports, they might pick an incompatible driver version or test against the wrong server features and see failures or degraded behavior.
improvements: Add a concise 'Supported wire protocol versions' box at the top of the compatibility reference (5.0–8.0) so agents don't fall back to older-version guesses.
In quickstarts include a tested driver version suggestion tied to each supported server version.

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: For local development use the official MongoDB Docker image (for the matching Mongo server version you target, e.g. mongo:7). The Mongo default port is 27017. The Azure Cosmos DB Emulator exists for Windows ... but for Mongo-specific development run a local mongo container: docker run -p 27017:27017 mongo:7.0.
confusions.grounded_answer: For Azure DocumentDB development the recommended local image is the DocumentDB Gateway Docker image (ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local:latest), which exposes the MongoDB-compatible wire protocol on port 10260 and requires TLS and the local cert. Use the Gateway image or docker-compose recipe provided in the documentdb-local-deployment guidance (not the generic mongo:7 image) for best parity.

grounding_links.title: documentdb-local-deployment
Local Deployment & Developer Workflow — Azure DocumentDB (skill content)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The model recommended a generic MongoDB container (27017), which is fine for general Mongo development, but Azure DocumentDB provides a dedicated Gateway image (10260 and TLS) to preserve feature parity with the managed cluster.
confusions.build_risk: Using a plain mongo container for local integration tests can hide compatibility differences the sample relies on (TLS, vector search, special features) and create false confidence in local tests.
improvements: Add a short note in tutorials: 'For local dev use the DocumentDB Gateway image; mongo:latest is insufficient to emulate DocumentDB feature set.'
Provide a minimal docker-compose example in the Mongoose quickstart referencing the Gateway image and port 10260.

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: Change streams are available on many Cosmos DB Mongo API compatibility versions. In many accounts you can use the MongoDB changeStream API (collection.watch()). There may be account/version prerequisites; in general nothing extra in-app must be enabled beyond using a compatible API version, but check the account's supported features if change streams are critical.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports change streams. Multishard change-stream features may require enabling cluster features (e.g., 'Change streams for multishard clusters' preview). The docs describe enabling Microsoft Entra ID and specific feature toggles for multi-shard change streams; regular change streams are available but account/cluster configuration should be verified.

grounding_links.title: Change streams in Azure DocumentDB (how-to & enable multishard preview)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: n/a

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the 'documentdb' MCP server profile to access data-plane inspection tools for DocumentDB/Cosmos Mongo API. The general Azure MCP server covers management-plane operations, but the 'documentdb' MCP server gives more targeted data-plane commands and inspectors for this service.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: the 'documentdb' MCP server provides data-plane tools (list_indexes, explain, find, insert, aggregate, create_index, etc.). The general Azure MCP server is for control plane/management-plane tasks; both exist but data-plane inspections use the documentdb server.

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: Microsoft originally shipped a service called Azure DocumentDB (the JSON document DB) which evolved and was renamed into Azure Cosmos DB. 'DocumentDB' as the old name is part of that history. Azure Cosmos DB exposes multiple APIs including a MongoDB-compatible API. The unrelated open-source 'DocumentDB' (if you mean other projects) is not the same as Microsoft's old service—Microsoft's DocumentDB became Cosmos DB.
confusions.grounded_answer: This area is easily confused. The current product 'Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)' was previously known as the vCore variant of 'Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore)' and has been rebranded; it is a distinct offering from the old 'Azure DocumentDB' (2014–2017) that became Azure Cosmos DB. Also, Azure DocumentDB (this product) is powered by the open-source DocumentDB engine — a separate open-source project — and is not the same as Amazon DocumentDB.

grounding_links.title: What is Azure DocumentDB (naming and history)
Azure DocumentDB at a glance (naming)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: There are several similarly named products over time (original Azure DocumentDB → renamed to Cosmos DB; Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore) rebranded to Azure DocumentDB). The model conflated historical names.

confusion_sources.title: Older blog posts and docs that refer to the older 'Azure DocumentDB' that became Cosmos DB

confusions.build_risk: If the repo used old naming/ARM types or guidance, a user or automation could target the wrong service or pick the wrong API/driver assumptions.
improvements: Add a succinct naming timeline to the top-level overview page showing: (1) original Azure DocumentDB → (2) Azure Cosmos DB; then (3) 'Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore)' → rebranded to 'Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)' to avoid ambiguous references.
Add a 'Which service is this?' banner to quickstarts that compares 'Azure DocumentDB (vCore)' vs 'Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (RU)' vs 'Amazon DocumentDB'.

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: Underneath is the Azure Cosmos DB service which implements the MongoDB wire protocol (a translation layer) rather than running upstream mongod behind the scenes for all accounts. That means you should use MongoDB drivers, but expect some behavioral and feature differences (aggregation / transactions / server-side features) compared with a stock MongoDB server; code that uses basic CRUD, indexes and common aggregations will usually work unchanged.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB is powered by the open-source DocumentDB engine (DocumentDB project) built on PostgreSQL; it implements MongoDB wire-protocol compatibility. Applications should use MongoDB drivers (Mongoose) and test features for compatibility because there are service-specific limits and differences, but many CRUD and aggregation patterns work unchanged. The key correction: the engine is DocumentDB (open-source) rather than 'Cosmos DB implementing the wire protocol'—the product is distinct and open-source-based.

grounding_links.title: DocumentDB: The Open-Source Engine Powering Azure DocumentDB
What is Azure DocumentDB? (overview)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The model assumed the more familiar Cosmos DB 'translation layer' story. The current product is built on the DocumentDB open-source engine and not simply 'Cosmos implementing the Mongo wire protocol'.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumed runtime behavior identical to Cosmos DB or to upstream mongod, some features (e.g., admin commands, specific platform-managed behavior) might behave differently; tests would show differences at runtime.
improvements: Add a short 'engine and implications' blurb in the overview and the quickstart: 'Powered by the open-source DocumentDB engine — drivers are the same but expect some platform-managed behaviors.'
Link the open-source project page prominently from the product overview to avoid mistaken assumptions.

confusions.question: How will tenant isolation be enforced in the repository layer?
confusions.cold_answer: Enforce tenant isolation by requiring tenantId as an explicit parameter for all repository methods and by always adding { tenantId } into the query filters before calling Mongoose/driver methods. Additionally register Mongoose query middleware (pre 'find'/'findOne'/'update' hooks) to assert tenantId presence or automatically inject a tenantId filter.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct and recommended: require tenantId in repository methods and inject/validate tenantId in a central place such as repository methods or Mongoose query middleware (pre hooks) to avoid cross-tenant queries. This approach is in line with best practices.

confusions.question: What TLS/connection options will the sample require when connecting to the live cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Require TLS: ensure the connection string includes tls/ssl=true (or use mongodb+srv which implies TLS). For Cosmos Mongo API include replicaSet=globaldb and retryWrites=false if needed. The sample will not disable TLS and will not connect without the DOCUMENTDB_URI containing the proper TLS options.
confusions.grounded_answer: Mostly correct for DocumentDB vCore clusters: use mongodb+srv (implies TLS) or include tls=true/ssl=true and authMechanism=SCRAM-SHA-256; many quickstart examples add retrywrites=false and maxIdleTimeMS options. Do not disable TLS. The exact additional options (replicaSet=globaldb) are not universally required for the vCore mongocluster SRV strings — follow the connection string provided by the cluster's 'list-connection-strings'.

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The model mixed general Cosmos Mongo API options (replicaSet=globaldb common in older Cosmos RU examples) with the vCore cluster SRV recommendations; cluster-provided connection strings are authoritative.
confusions.build_risk: If the sample unhelpfully mutates or validates DOCUMENTDB_URI expecting certain query parameters, it could break SRV-style URIs or fail to honor the cluster-provided string.
improvements: In the quickstart, show the exact sample SRV connection string and recommend the app to use the given connection string unchanged (do not parse/edit SRV entries).
Add a short 'Do not alter the cluster-provided URI' note in the sample README and .env.example.

information_gaps.title: Seed dataset shape and tenants
information_gaps.description: The prompt doesn't specify sample data (how many tenants, products per tenant, SKUs shape, inventory records, or order patterns). The builder must invent an idempotent seed script. I checked the sample prompt and installed skills; none prescribe a specific dataset shape or sample contents.

information_gaps.title: Mongoose / mongodb driver exact version to pin
information_gaps.description: The prompt didn't pin Mongoose or mongodb driver versions. Microsoft tutorials suggest Mongoose 9.x and tested driver versions in docs, but there's no single pinned version enforced by the agent skills. I checked the Mongoose quickstart docs which recommend Mongoose 9.12.1 in examples, but the sample prompt left the decision to the builder.

information_gaps.title: Repository API surface (REST vs CLI)
information_gaps.description: Prompt leaves open whether to produce an Express REST API or a CLI/library. The prompt review assumed an Express API will be produced; no skill or doc mandates this. The builder must confirm API surface with the author or pick a convention.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Use the Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters resource type for ARM/Bicep/Terraform when referring to or provisioning the target cluster (do not use Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts).

Use the 'az documentdb mongocluster' CLI commands (install the documentdb extension if needed) or the documentdb MCP server to inspect cluster connection strings, list indexes, and create cluster-level settings; do not attempt to manage this vCore cluster using databaseAccounts/az cosmosdb account commands.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Read the cluster connection string from process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI and pass it unchanged to mongoose.connect(); do not rewrite SRV URIs or inject database-specific query parameters — use the cluster-provided connection string.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Create the requested compound indexes explicitly before accepting traffic: products (tenantId:1, sku:1) [unique if SKU uniqueness per tenant is required], orders (tenantId:1, createdAt:-1), inventory (tenantId:1, sku:1). Verify index creation with documentdb.list_indexes or with the MCP server.

Enforce tenant isolation centrally: require tenantId on every repository method and inject tenantId into query filters (or enforce via Mongoose pre middleware) so no repository call can return or mutate documents for a different tenant.

inventory_recommendations.name: azd
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required to build this Node.js sample; az (already installed) and the documentdb MCP server suffice. If desired for richer dev-to-cloud workflows, install Azure Developer CLI (azd) via its official installer.

inventory_recommendations.name: bicep
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Bicep is useful for IaC but not required for this sample (the run policy forbids provisioning). If the team later wants to include IaC examples, install the Bicep CLI (az bicep) or run az cli bicep commands.

inventory_recommendations.name: terraform
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Terraform is useful to produce deployable IaC but the current run policy forbids Azure writes and the sample uses an existing cluster. Add Terraform only if you intend to include provisioning examples; otherwise rely on documentdb MCP and the Azure docs.

inventory_recommendations.name: dotnet
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for this Node.js sample. If cross-language samples are planned, install dotnet SDK through official installers.

inventory_recommendations.name: mongosh
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: mongosh is useful for interactive debugging and for manual verification of indexes and queries. Install mongosh to make it easy for developers to inspect the cluster outside the MCP server. If mongosh cannot be installed, the documentdb MCP server supplies equivalent programmatic inspection tools (list_indexes, explain, find).
